newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU avoids defining recession in EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU avoids defining recession in EMU pact.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday left unspecified the economic conditions under which a country joining a common European currency could run excessive deficits without facing stiff penalties.

Speaking at a news conference, Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said there was broad agreement that a proposed budget stability pact should include tough fines on governments running annual deficits above three percent of total output.

But it remained possible that sanctions might be avoided because of extraordinary economic circumstances -- an economic shock or severe recession -- though these were not defined. The fines should be applied in a semi-automatic fashion, a feature that is absent from the EU's current procedure for dealing with lax budget policies.
"The most important aspect is not the penalty aspect but the prevention aspect," de Silguy said, outlining the Commission's views on several areas of monetary union.

Specifically, the Commission proposed an initial fixed fine of 0.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a further 0.1 percent of output for every percentage point a country's deficit rose above the three percent limit.
In addition, the maximum fine the EU could impose on EMU members with excessive budget deficits would be 0.5 percent of GDP.
Under the scenario outlined, a government which was deemed to have an excessive deficit would have 10 months to introduce adequate measures to bring down its deficit.
On the controversial issue of what economic conditions would allow governments to escape sanctions, the Commission backed down from an earlier proposal of an annual 1.5 percent decline in real GDP.
Instead, de Silguy said the circumstances in each country would have to be analysed and that differences between countries precluded putting exact figures on what constituted a severe recession.

The proposed budget pact is considered an essential feature of economic and monetary union (EMU), designed to ensure budgetary discipline among governments joining the single currency, the euro, expected in 1999.
Officials said there was strong resistance from several southern European countries to an explicit definition of a severe recession.
EU monetary officials were cautious in their reaction to the Commission's plan, with some suggesting it left too many loopholes which governments might use to avoid sanctions.
In particular, the proposed regulation says EU finance ministers would "as a rule, decide to impose sanctions" if a country failed to rectify its deficit problem.
Yet in earlier drafts, prepared by the EU's monetary committee, the relevant clause stated that there was a "presumption" that fines would be levied, legally a much stronger version, officials said.
"Where there is a rule there are exceptions," said one official.
The Commission also unveiled its views on reinforced economic convergence procedures for countries not participating in the single currency at the start.
The proposed strengthening of such procedures along with a new Exchange Rate Mechanism is expected to enhance monetary stability in the EU after the euro's launch.
Lastly, a legal framework for the euro was proposed. Its primary objectives are to ensure legal certainty for businesses and financial markets after 1999.

The Commission will attempt to bring forward legislation which assures the continuity of contracts under EMU, establishes a one-for-one conversion rate between Ecu contracts and the euro, legally enforces euro as the single currency' name, and makes clear certain rounding rules.
All of the proposals will be discussed by European Finance Ministers in the coming weeks with a final agreement expected by the time of the summit of EU leaders in Dublin in December.
